strengths: The paper targets an important problem: causal discovery when interactions vary over time according to latent, potentially variable-specific states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive and compact alternative to enumerating K^N global regimes.

SDCI is a technically interesting combination of amortized graph inference, discrete-state modeling, and shared pairwise interaction functions. Considering observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent states within one framework is useful.

The evaluation spans physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene regulation, and NBA trajectories. The determined-state experiments show promising structural recovery, and the paper is reasonably candid about difficulties in the recurrent setting and the lack of estimator-consistency guarantees.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with helpful diagrams and substantial appendices covering architectures, datasets, and training settings; code is linked. Review based on the complete source PDF :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-cbtby5jh/call-018e149681354db0b01177cc6ce78cfc/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central identifiability argument is not valid as stated. Theorem A.6 invokes pointwise finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability without assuming positive mixing weights or reachability of every regime. In the paper's deterministic-state setting, conditional regime weights can be 0 or 1; unused components, their graphs, and even K are then unidentifiable. Adding an unreachable regime with a distinct graph leaves the observed distribution unchanged, directly contradicting the claimed result and the assertion that no assumption on state dependence is needed.

The edge-type result has another major proof gap. Corollary A.8 claims permutation invariance makes the derivatives of the aggregator equal across messages and targets. This is false in general—for example, a sum of squared messages is permutation invariant but has input-dependent derivatives. Moreover, equality of products involving unknown derivatives of g and f_e does not establish a single global permutation of edge types. Considerably stronger additive, injective, and support assumptions would be needed.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is unconvincing. In the stated generative factorization, s_t affects x_{t+1}, so p(s_t|x_{1:T},W) includes the next-step likelihood and is generally not p_psi(s_t|x_t). Equation 57 also appears to move elementwise state sums through a nonlinear aggregation function and Gaussian likelihood; the exact marginal normally retains K^N combinations. This undermines the objective and implementation characterization.

The theoretical scope is substantially overstated. Results require no confounding, no instantaneous effects, first-order dynamics, Gaussian independent noise, faithfulness, a distinct outgoing adjacency for every state of every variable, and globally shared finite interaction types. These conditions are neither enforced by the unconstrained neural architecture nor shown to hold in the experiments, and consistency of the actual variational estimator is explicitly left open.

The experiments do not adequately test the main causal-discovery claim. The principal baseline comparison on particles uses only determined states and evaluates the union summary graph, not recovery of the proposed conditional graph. The harder recurrent case has no corresponding causal-baseline comparison. Fixed-graph perfect recovery uses a globally parameterized graph learned from 10,000 samples and is not compelling evidence for per-sample discovery.

The GRN evidence comes from one simulator configuration that assumes longitudinal measurements of the same synthetic cell. Headline values lack reported repetitions or uncertainty, F1 is threshold-sensitive, and Rhino essentially matches the best AUROC. The R-PCMCI evaluation uses defaults after the authors report implementation failures, limiting the credibility of that comparison. NBA data provide no causal ground truth; small forecasting differences and post-hoc visual interpretations cannot validate causal edges or latent regimes.

The unknown-K claim is supported only by two visually selected elbow curves, without a selection rule, recovery-rate experiment, or repeated trials. More generally, seeds, the meaning of plotted error bars, threshold selection, and permutation alignment for latent-state and edge-type F1 scores are unspecified. These issues, together with inconsistent edge-direction/state-index notation in the particle description, impede informed reproduction.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult setting: causal discovery when lagged interactions change according to latent, potentially observation-dependent states. The conditional summary graph is a useful compact representation of source-specific state-dependent structure, avoiding explicit enumeration of K^N global regimes.

SDCI is a reasonably coherent extension of amortized graph inference, combining discrete state variables, typed edges, and message-passing dynamics. Considering observed, determined, and recurrent states provides a helpful organization of the problem.

The evaluation is broad, covering controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories. Some results are encouraging, particularly the synthetic fixed-structure recovery and the improved GRN F1 score of the determined-state model.

The manuscript is generally readable, relates the proposal to relevant switching-model and causal-discovery literature, supplies substantial implementation and dataset detail, and points to public code.
weaknesses: The central identifiability argument has a serious gap. Theorem A.6 applies finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability at each conditioning history without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. Determined states can produce zero-one weights, while recurrent processes may contain unreachable regimes; such components, their graphs, and even their number cannot be recovered this way. The subsequent move from an input-dependent component matching to one global permutation is also not rigorously established.

The proof of conditional-effect label identifiability appears invalid. Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across messages and targets. Permutation invariance does not imply this: for a symmetric function such as a sum of squared messages, the derivatives vary with the individual message values. Equation 47 therefore does not isolate the derivatives of the edge-type functions, and the claimed single global permutation of edge labels does not follow. This directly affects Theorem 4.3, a principal contribution.

The connection between the assumptions and SDCI is unsubstantiated. Analyticity alone does not guarantee assumption (a2.2), especially with its existential quantifier over the second input, and the implemented edge functions are Leaky-ReLU MLPs rather than analytic functions. Unique outgoing structures and functional faithfulness are likewise not verified for the experimental generators or learned models.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is questionable. A source state jointly controls all its outgoing messages, and the nonlinear aggregator couples messages from multiple sources; marginalizing the observation likelihood therefore generally requires joint state combinations. Equation 57 instead factorizes these coupled quantities. Moreover, setting q(s_t|x_1:T)=p(s_t|x_t) is not the exact posterior when future observations also depend on s_t, unless the state is truly deterministic.

The empirical comparisons do not adequately test the main state-conditioned discovery claim. Conditional graphs and typed labels are quantitatively evaluated only for SDCI, while the principal baseline comparison collapses them to a union summary graph and mostly uses methods assuming stationarity. Relevant regime-switching approaches are not compared on the central synthetic tasks, and recurrent variable-graph recovery is already weak at small scale.

Statistical evidence is incomplete: the number of random seeds is unspecified, several headline plots and the GRN table lack uncertainty, most synthetic results are not tabulated, and threshold/model-selection details are insufficient. R-PCMCI is used with defaults after tuning failures, making its very low F1 difficult to interpret. Two hand-selected reconstruction-error curves do not substantiate reliable recovery of K, particularly since the displayed quantity is test error rather than a validation selection criterion.

The NBA study has no causal ground truth, uses hand-designed states, and likely violates causal sufficiency and the first-order lag assumptions. Slight forecasting improvements and visually plausible dense graphs therefore support predictive usefulness at most, not the paper's causal or interpretability claims. Overall, the appealing formulation and promising experiments constitute substantive merit, but the theoretical defects and incomplete validation undermine the principal conclusions enough to favor rejection.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored setting: causal discovery when interactions change according to latent, potentially observation-dependent states.

The conditional summary graph is a useful compact representation. Under the paper's source-state factorization, it reduces a potentially exponential collection of global regime graphs to K state-indexed graphs.

SDCI is a coherent combination of discrete latent-state modeling, amortized graph inference, and GNN dynamics. The evaluation spans physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene networks, and real trajectories, including fixed and sample-varying graphs.
The synthetic results suggest that the approach can recover useful structure in favorable settings. The appendix provides substantial architectural and training detail, and code is referenced.
weaknesses: The central identifiability argument is not convincing. Theorem A.6 applies finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability at each fixed history without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability on a common support. In the emphasized determined-state case, the regime can be a deterministic function of the observation, so all but one mixture weight may be zero at each conditioning value. Unvisited regimes and their graphs can then be changed without affecting the observed distribution, invalidating the claimed recovery of U/K and the regime graphs under the stated assumptions.

Corollary A.8 contains another major gap: permutation invariance of the aggregator does not imply that its partial derivatives are equal across message arguments or target nodes; for example, a symmetric nonlinear aggregator can have input-dependent derivatives. Moreover, equality of products involving derivatives of g and the edge functions does not identify the edge-function labels without additional restrictions. Thus the claimed single global permutation of edge types does not follow.

The claimed O(NK) exact inference for determined states in Eq. 57 appears incorrect. A source state s_i is shared by all outgoing messages, so marginalizing it generally couples multiple targets; separate per-edge sums implicitly introduce independent copies of that state. A nonlinear aggregation also prevents replacing joint marginalization with marginal messages. Likewise, p(s_t|x_t) is generally not the smoothing posterior once future observations generated from s_t are observed. These issues undermine the stated likelihood/ELBO interpretation.

The advertised scope is considerably broader than the implemented model. Each edge may depend only on the source node's state, while Eq. 11 makes each state process depend only on that node's own observations and state history. Dependence on target states, global context, or other agents' histories is excluded, alongside hidden confounding, instantaneous effects, higher-order dynamics, and non-Gaussian noise. The strong unique-outgoing-structure assumption is also not shown to hold in the experiments and is implausible for nodes with no outgoing edges, such as GRN target genes.

The main empirical comparisons do not directly validate the main object of interest. Baselines are largely evaluated on the union summary graph, while conditional-graph and state recovery are reported only for SDCI. Relevant regime-switching baselines are not quantitatively compared on the controlled physical experiments, and there are no ablations separating the benefits of latent states, additional edge-to-edge layers, increased capacity, or state supervision.

Empirical support is insufficiently quantified: most results omit run-to-run uncertainty, seed counts, statistical tests, and exact threshold-selection procedures. On GRNs, the best AUROC is only 0.936 versus Rhino's 0.933 without uncertainty, while the best F1 remains 0.347 and baseline capacities appear mismatched. On NBA, gains over ACD are slight and lack uncertainty; forecasting accuracy and qualitative dense graphs do not establish causal validity. The K-selection claim is supported by only two examples where reconstruction error merely plateaus, leaving the true K ambiguous.

SDCI is a coherent extension of amortized graph inference, combining discrete latent states, typed interactions, and a permutation-invariant GNN decoder. Treating observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent states in one framework is useful.

The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks, and NBA trajectories. SDCI performs strongly in several synthetic settings and obtains the best reported GRN F1 score.

The manuscript is well organized and visually polished. It states many modeling assumptions explicitly, provides substantial architectural and training detail, releases code, and candidly acknowledges the lack of an estimator-consistency result and the difficulty of recurrent-state inference.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability theorem does not follow as stated. Theorem A.6 applies finite-mixture identifiability without requiring positive conditional mixture weights or sufficient regime support. Determined states may give a point-mass p(u|x), recurrent states may never visit some regimes, and dependent per-variable states need not realize all K^N configurations. An unvisited state's graph can be changed without changing p(x_1:T), directly contradicting the claimed identifiability and recovery of unknown K.

The proof of edge-type identifiability has another major gap. It asserts that permutation invariance of g makes its partial derivatives with respect to different messages equal. This is false for a general permutation-invariant function—for example, a sum of squared messages. Moreover, assumption (a2.2) distinguishes edge functions only within each model and does not exclude compensating reparameterizations of f and g across observationally equivalent models. Thus Corollary A.8 does not establish a single global permutation of edge labels.

Definition 4.1/A.3 is internally inconsistent: Eq. (17) states that an edge label equals its permuted counterpart if and only if it is zero. With one nonzero edge type, the nonzero permutation is necessarily the identity, making Eqs. (17) and (18) contradictory. This may be a notation error, but it affects the central theorem's formal meaning.

The claimed O(NK) exact inference for determined states is not justified. A source state s_i jointly selects all outgoing messages from node i, coupling multiple target likelihoods. Equation (57) effectively moves products over targets through separate state sums and loses this coupling. Unless states are truly deterministic or stronger factorization assumptions hold, q_s=p_s is also not the posterior because future observations contain information about s.

The assumptions are substantially narrower than the framing suggests: fully observed variables, no confounding or instantaneous effects, first-order Gaussian additive noise, source-state-only switching, globally shared edge functions, and unique outgoing topology for every state of every variable. Assumption (a1) excludes regimes that change interaction strength but not adjacency and appears violated by GRN target genes with no outgoing edges; the paper does not verify it for the experimental generators.

The experiments do not adequately test the central conditional-graph contribution against appropriate alternatives. Direct W recovery is reported only for SDCI on the custom particle simulator. Comparisons in Figure 6 and Table 1 collapse the output to an ordinary summary graph, discarding state-specific structure. Relevant switching/regime baselines are largely absent from the controlled experiments, and there is no ablation separating latent-state modeling from increased architecture or capacity.

The empirical comparisons lack robustness. Most main results provide no variation over independent training seeds or statistical tests, several results are available only as plots, and baseline configurations are uneven—for example, Rhino uses a much smaller network, while R-PCMCI uses defaults after tuning attempts failed. The unknown-K claim is supported only by an informal elbow plot on two selected simulations, not systematic recovery rates or likelihood-based model selection.

The NBA experiment validates forecasting rather than causality: it has no causal ground truth, likely violates the stated causal assumptions, shows only small unquantified differences from ACD, and interprets dense learned edges post hoc. The GRN data are also simulated and rely on longitudinal measurements of the same cell that real single-cell experiments generally cannot provide. strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored setting. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive and potentially useful representation that exploits source-specific states to replace an exponentially large collection of regime graphs with K state-indexed graphs.

SDCI is a coherent synthesis of amortized graph inference, discrete latent-state modeling, and GNN interaction functions. Treating observed, observation-determined, and recurrent states in one framework is practically appealing.

The evaluation spans controlled particle dynamics, a 49-gene DynGen simulation, and large-scale NBA trajectories. Several results are promising, notably the DynGen F1 score of 0.347 for determined-state SDCI versus 0.187 for ACD, and strong recovery on fixed-graph particle systems.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, discusses relevant recent work, supplies substantial implementation and dataset detail in the appendix, and provides code. It also candidly notes limitations involving variational consistency and recurrent-state inference. The complete source was inspected: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pek0pcdg/call-c5216645b5904969a9c7f90d89ab37e2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Major: The central identifiability argument does not cover arbitrary state dependence as claimed. Applying finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability in Theorem A.6 requires the relevant mixture components to have positive weight. No positivity, support, or visitation assumption is imposed, and determined states can give 0/1 weights at each conditioning value. Unvisited regimes can be changed without altering p(x_1:T), so U=K^N and hence K need not be identifiable. This gap propagates to Theorem A.7 and Corollary A.8.

Major: The proof of edge-type identifiability contains an unjustified step. Permutation invariance of g does not imply that its partial derivatives with respect to different messages are equal across i and j; a generic symmetric function already provides counterexamples, and the implemented sum-then-MLP derivative still depends on the target and aggregate. Assumptions (a2.1-a2.2) also do not rule out compensation between the unknown derivatives of g and the edge functions. Consequently, the claimed single global permutation of nonzero edge labels is not established.

Major: Appendix B.2's claimed O(NK) exact marginalization for determined states appears incorrect for the nonlinear aggregator. The observation likelihood remains a mixture over K^N joint state configurations, and expected messages generally cannot be passed through g or the Gaussian likelihood. Moreover, p(s_t|x_t) is not the full posterior when the likelihood of x_{t+1} also informs s_t, unless the state mapping is truly deterministic. The paper should either impose conditions making this exact or characterize the computation as an approximation.

The empirical comparison does not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Most baselines assume stationarity; the principal regime-aware baseline, R-PCMCI, is used only on one GRN dataset with default settings after tuning reportedly failed. There is no parameter-matched latent-state forecasting baseline or ablation separating extra state capacity from conditional causal structure. Most plots also omit independent-run variability, and state-label alignment, graph threshold selection, and selection of K are insufficiently specified.

The real-data evidence cannot validate causal discovery. NBA states are hand-designed or learned from position, causal graphs have no ground truth, interpretations are qualitative, and the forecast advantage over ACD is small and lacks uncertainty; prediction alone cannot establish a causality-driven benefit. The GRN study uses one simulated topology and simulator-internal longitudinal measurements of the same cells, which the paper itself notes are unavailable in real single-cell sequencing, so the biological applicability claim is premature.

The advertised scope is broader than the supported setting: the model excludes hidden confounding and instantaneous effects, assumes first-order dynamics, isotropic Gaussian noise, unique outgoing structures for every source/state, and globally shared interaction types. The implementation further restricts each state transition to the corresponding variable's own history while adding dataset-specific node embeddings. These assumptions and theory-implementation differences need clearer qualification. Overall, the representation and algorithm are promising, but the unsupported central theorems and limited causal validation make rejection more appropriate in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored problem: causal discovery when relationships change according to latent, variable-specific states.
The conditional summary graph is an intuitive compact alternative to enumerating K^N global regimes, and SDCI coherently combines state inference, state-indexed edges, and nonlinear GNN dynamics.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled particle systems, a 49-gene DynGen simulation, and NBA trajectories. Results are particularly strong in the determined-state synthetic settings, and the paper candidly reports difficulty in recurrent settings.
The presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The appendix supplies architectural and training details, and a code repository is provided.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result lacks a positivity, reachability, or regime-overlap assumption. In Eq. 35, context-dependent mixture weights may be zero—especially for deterministically assigned states—so pointwise Gaussian-mixture identifiability cannot imply recovery of U, K, or never-active regimes. This directly undermines the claimed guarantee with unrestricted state dependencies.

Corollary A.8 does not convincingly establish identifiability of edge-type labels. Permutation invariance of g does not imply equal partial derivatives at unequal message values or across targets, and separately learned g and f functions permit transformations not excluded by assumptions (a2.1-a2.2). Definition 4.1/Eq. 17 also appears logically malformed: it should preserve zero labels rather than equate labels iff one is zero.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is insufficiently justified. With a nonlinear aggregator, state choices for multiple incoming messages remain coupled; Eq. 57 does not perform the required joint marginalization. Moreover, q(s_t|x_t)=p(s_t|x_t) is the posterior only under an explicitly deterministic state map, since s_t also affects future observations.

The experiments do not directly compare conditional-summary-graph or edge-type recovery against matched regime-switching alternatives. The main baseline comparison instead unions conditional graphs into an ordinary summary graph, discarding the paper's central state-conditioned output. Several closely related cited methods and a same-capacity latent-regime ablation are absent.

The applied evidence does not establish the broader causal claims. On DynGen, the best F1 is only 0.347 and the best AUROC is essentially tied with Rhino; AUPRC, threshold selection, run-to-run variation, and significance are not reported. NBA has no causal ground truth, and its small forecasting improvement could arise from extra latent-state capacity rather than correct causal discovery.

The practical scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the model assumes causal sufficiency, no instantaneous effects, first-order dynamics, source-state-only modulation, and globally shared pairwise effect types. Given the unsupported central theorem and indirect evaluation of the principal discovery task, rejection is presently more appropriate despite the promising formulation.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is a useful and intuitive abstraction: exploiting source-specific states reduces the representation from K^N global regimes to K state-indexed graphs while retaining state-dependent outgoing structure.

SDCI combines discrete state inference, edge-type discovery, and graph-based dynamics in a coherent framework covering observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent states, including graphs that vary between samples.

The evaluation spans controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene regulation, and real basketball trajectories. Several results are promising, particularly the summary-graph performance on particle data and F1 improvement on the DynGen network.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, openly discusses some limitations, supplies substantial architectural and training detail, and provides code. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-0quttsga/call-3fdc7f93f34946ec91e67c443a144650/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not established under the stated assumptions. Theorem A.6 invokes finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability at each conditioning history without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. Arbitrary state dependence explicitly permits zero-weight or deterministic regimes—as in the paper's determined-state examples—so inactive components and even additional never-used states cannot be identified. This directly undermines the claims of requiring no assumptions on state dependence and identifying an unknown K.

The proof of edge-type identifiability contains another consequential gap. Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of g makes its partial derivatives with respect to different messages equal. This is false in general; for example, a permutation-invariant sum of squared messages has message-dependent derivatives. The unknown interaction functions and aggregator can also compensate for one another. Assumptions (a2.1–a2.2) therefore do not justify a single global permutation of nonzero edge labels. The accompanying assertion that analyticity guarantees (a2.2) is also incorrect without stronger restrictions.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is insufficiently justified. In the generative graph, future observations generally update the posterior of s_t, so p(s_t|x_t) is not p(s_t|x_1:T,W) unless the state is genuinely deterministic. Moreover, marginalizing independent local states through a nonlinear aggregation and Gaussian decoder generally entails a sum over joint state configurations; Eq. 57 does not show that this marginal factorizes.

The empirical comparisons only partly test the principal contribution. Particle baselines are evaluated on the union summary graph rather than the conditional summary graph or edge-type tensor W, and the hardest recurrent, variable-graph setting lacks meaningful baseline comparisons while SDCI itself performs modestly. There are no ablations isolating state inference, edge-to-edge attention, or the sparsity prior, and R-PCMCI is run with defaults after tuning failures.

Experimental uncertainty and selection procedures are inadequately reported. The paper does not clearly state the number of independent training runs, define the plotted error bars, report variability for the GRN and NBA results, or specify F1 threshold selection. The single DynGen configuration yields low absolute F1, and the surprising advantage of inferred states over supplied states is not investigated.

The evidence for selecting K consists of two reconstruction-error curves that plateau after the true K; this does not uniquely recover K and provides no quantitative model-selection test. Likewise, NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth and shows only small predictive differences, so hand-crafted or learned spatial partitions and qualitative graphs cannot substantiate causal discovery or causality-driven forecasting claims. The train/test split should also be specified at the game level to rule out leakage between overlapping trajectory segments.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important and underexplored setting: causal discovery when interaction structure changes with latent, local states. The conditional summary graph is a useful representation that avoids explicitly enumerating K^N global regimes. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-kkm2w5u0/call-52330a7413a94801afe44648c954da3c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SDCI forms a coherent model by combining per-variable discrete states, state-conditioned edge types, amortized graph inference, and GNN interaction aggregation. The distinction between observed, determined, and recurrent states is conceptually helpful.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene-regulatory networks, and real NBA trajectories. Results are promising in fixed-graph and determined-state synthetic settings, and the GRN experiment shows a meaningful F1 improvement over the reported baselines.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, provides extensive implementation and dataset details, links code, and candidly acknowledges difficulties with recurrent-state inference and the absence of an estimator-consistency result.
weaknesses: The central identifiability argument lacks a necessary positivity, reachability, or overlap assumption. Equation 35 is treated as a U-component Gaussian mixture, but in the emphasized determined-state case, s is a function of the observations, so only one regime can have nonzero weight at a given history. Arbitrary state dynamics can likewise make regimes unreachable. Finite-mixture identifiability then cannot establish the number of regimes or align all components by one permutation. This undermines Theorems A.6, A.7, and 4.3, particularly the claims of allowing unrestricted state dependence and identifying unknown K.

The proof of Corollary A.8 does not convincingly establish a global permutation of nonzero edge-type labels. Permutation invariance of an aggregator does not imply that its partial derivatives are equal across distinct messages or targets, and equality of products involving unknown derivatives of g and the edge functions does not imply equality of the edge-function derivatives. Assumption (a2.2) does not close this gap; the statement that analytic implementations automatically satisfy it is also too strong.

The theory concerns population identifiability of a restricted generative family, not recovery by the proposed variational estimator. The paper explicitly leaves SDCI consistency open, while mean-field factorization and approximate recurrent inference can introduce further failures. Consequently, describing the finite synthetic study as empirically verifying consistency overstates what it establishes.

The main causal comparison on particles evaluates only the union summary graph and primarily uses stationary baselines that are deliberately misspecified for the generated data. There is no strong regime-switching baseline on this controlled task, despite such methods being discussed, nor an ablation separating benefits from latent states, added encoder capacity, edge-to-edge attention, and sparsity priors.

Experimental uncertainty is insufficiently documented: the number of independent training seeds and the meaning of several error bars are not reported, while many results have no uncertainty estimates. Threshold selection is also unclear; in the GRN table, Rhino nearly matches SDCI's AUROC but has a dramatically lower F1, making the claimed structural advantage sensitive to an unspecified thresholding protocol.

The real-data evidence does not validate causal discovery. NBA has no causal ground truth, its learned graphs receive only qualitative interpretation, and the forecasting gain over ACD is small and confounded by architectural and training differences. The GRN result uses one simulator configuration and still has modest absolute F1. Likewise, the unknown-K claim is supported only by two visually selected reconstruction-error plateaus rather than a specified and repeatedly evaluated model-selection procedure.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: causal discovery when interactions change over time. The conditional summary graph is a useful, interpretable representation that reduces K^N global regimes to K source-state-conditioned graphs.
SDCI coherently combines discrete latent-state modeling, amortized graph inference, and shared GNN interaction mechanisms, covering observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent state settings.

The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, a biologically motivated simulator, and real multi-agent trajectories. Synthetic results show promising structure recovery, particularly for fixed graphs and determined states.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams, extensive implementation details, public code, and a reasonably broad discussion of related work and limitations.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result lacks essential positivity, visitation, and support assumptions. With determined states, p(s|x) can be one-hot, so the conditional distribution contains only one active Gaussian component at each x; finite-mixture identifiability cannot recover K^N components. More simply, an unvisited state can have an arbitrary graph without changing p(x), contradicting identification of its graph or K.

Several proof steps are insufficiently justified. Pointwise Gaussian-mixture identifiability only supplies a permutation that may vary with the conditioning value, and the argument making it globally constant is incomplete. In Corollary A.8, permutation invariance of g does not imply equal partial derivatives at different message values or targets, so it does not establish one global edge-type permutation. The implemented unconstrained leaky-ReLU networks also do not guarantee the stated derivative assumptions.

There is a mismatch between theory and the proposed estimator: the theorem effectively treats W as fixed, whereas the generative model samples and marginalizes a different W for each sequence. It therefore does not identify a sample-specific latent graph from a single trajectory, as claimed.

The claimed exact O(NK) state inference in the determined case is questionable. Because the observation decoder nonlinearly aggregates all state-dependent messages, marginalizing states generally requires a joint sum; evaluating the decoder at averaged messages is not exact marginalization. Moreover, p_psi(s_t|x_t) is not the full posterior once future observations depend on s_t.

Experimental reporting is not sufficiently robust. The number of training seeds is unspecified, several central results lack uncertainty, and the latent-state and edge-type F1 calculations do not explain the permutation alignment required by the paper's own identifiability definition. Threshold selection for graph F1 is also unclear.

The comparisons provide limited evidence for state-dependent causal discovery. Most spring baselines assume stationarity and are evaluated only on the union summary graph; non-amortized methods are retrained on individual short sequences, and R-PCMCI uses defaults after tuning failures. Oracle-state segmentation, capacity-matched latent-state baselines, and ablations isolating the graph/state components are missing.

The real-data evidence does not validate causal structure: NBA has no causal ground truth and the small forecasting improvement could come from additional latent capacity, while the GRN experiment uses one semi-synthetic, longitudinal same-cell setting and obtains only moderate best F1. Corresponding causal and biological claims are therefore overstated.

Despite broad framing, the model assumes first-order lagged effects, Gaussian additive independent noise, no hidden confounders or instantaneous effects, source-local states, and factorized state dynamics. The two illustrative elbow plots for K do not substantiate reliable unknown-state-number selection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: causal discovery when interactions change with latent, variable-specific states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive, compact alternative to enumerating K^N global regimes. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-5jp_sbn0/call-e1ba2fdf69a54b669e53be2d0ff170ad/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SDCI combines latent-state inference, typed-edge discovery, amortization across samples, and a permutation-invariant interaction decoder in a coherent framework. The distinction among observed, determined, and recurrent states is useful.

The evaluation spans controlled particle systems, a biologically motivated DynGen simulation, and NBA trajectories. Results are strong in the fixed-graph and determined-state synthetic settings, and the GRN experiment suggests potential practical value.
The relationship to ACD, switching dynamical systems, and nonstationary causal discovery is discussed reasonably well. Figures clearly communicate the representation and model.

The appendices provide architectures, optimization settings, data-generation details, and a code link. The authors also appropriately acknowledge the lack of an estimator-consistency result and the exponential cost of exact recurrent-state inference.
weaknesses: The main identifiability argument lacks a necessary state-occupancy condition. Theorem A.6 applies finite-mixture identifiability pointwise in the history, but arbitrary state dynamics can assign zero probability to some regimes; in the determined case the conditional mixture is typically degenerate. Zero-weight components, their graphs, and even K cannot be identified. Assumptions (a1)-(a2) constrain component mechanisms but do not ensure that every state or K^N configuration is observable, directly undermining the claimed guarantees for arbitrary state dependence and unknown K.

Corollary A.8 contains a substantive proof error. Permutation invariance of g does not imply that its partial derivatives are equal across messages or target variables; for example, a symmetric nonlinear aggregator can have input-dependent derivatives. Moreover, equality of products involving derivatives of g and f_e does not identify f_e because transformations can be absorbed by g. Thus the asserted single global permutation of edge types does not follow from (a2). Related claims that GNN message passing automatically satisfies (a2.1) and analyticity guarantees (a2.2) are false, and the implemented leaky-ReLU networks are not analytic anyway.

The claimed exact inference for determined states is insufficiently justified. Given the full sequence, a latent state generally receives evidence from the future observation it helps generate, so q(s_t|x_t)=p_s(s_t|x_t) is not the exact posterior unless the state map is truly deterministic. Equations (57)-(58) also do not correctly marginalize the jointly coupled messages through nonlinear g; substituting averaged or sampled messages as in Eq. (16) is not exact marginalization.

There is a large theory-algorithm gap. The distribution-level results assume faithful Gaussian ANMs, distinct globally shared effect functions, no hidden confounding or instantaneous effects, first-order dynamics, and ideal access to the observational distribution. SDCI neither enforces the identifiability assumptions nor has a consistency guarantee, while its state decoder imposes autonomous, variable-local dynamics that exclude some cross-agent dependencies used to motivate the work.

The central empirical comparison is not well matched to the claim. Most baselines assume stationarity and can only return an aggregated summary graph, so they do not test conditional-graph recovery. For variable graphs, Rhino and N-GC are retrained on each length-80 trajectory while SDCI amortizes over 10,000 training samples. Relevant switching or regime-discovery methods, oracle-state decompositions, and comparably amortized alternatives are largely absent.

Experimental reporting is too limited for firm conclusions: seed counts are unspecified, several principal plots lack uncertainty or numerical tables, threshold selection for F1 is unclear, and permutation alignment for state and edge labels is not documented. The GRN result uses one simulated backbone, and the large AUROC/F1 discrepancies suggest strong sensitivity to thresholding.

Evidence for the difficult recurrent and high-dimensional cases is weak. Recovery degrades even for small variable-graph particle systems, the 49-gene recurrent model requires batch size one, and no runtime or memory analysis is provided. Observed-state edge accuracy also approaches chance as K and N increase.

The NBA study establishes only predictive fit, not causal discovery. The advantage over ACD appears small and has no uncertainty analysis; the states are spatial partitions and the dense learned graphs receive only post-hoc interpretation. The train/test split protocol is insufficiently described to rule out leakage across overlapping plays or games. Likewise, unknown-K support consists only of a subjective reconstruction-error elbow on two synthetic examples. Overall, the representation and method have merit, but the invalid or incomplete central theory and inconclusive validation make rejection more appropriate at present.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is an intuitive and useful representation that reduces the description of state-dependent interactions from exponentially many joint regimes to K per-state graphs.
SDCI provides a coherent practical framework combining amortized graph inference, discrete latent states, and graph neural dynamics for observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent states.

The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene networks, and real NBA trajectories. Results are promising, including near-perfect fixed-graph recovery and the best reported GRN F1 score.
The manuscript is generally clear, supplies substantial implementation detail and an appendix, and links to code.
weaknesses: The central edge-label identifiability result is not established. Corollary A.8 incorrectly argues that permutation invariance makes derivatives with respect to different messages equal. For example, a permutation-invariant aggregator g({h_i}) = sum_i h_i^2 with f1(x)=x and f2(x)=-x satisfies the stated derivative-separation conditions but makes the two edge types observationally indistinguishable; independently swapping types on selected edges violates the claimed single global permutation.

The unknown-K and arbitrary-state-dependence claims omit essential regime-occupancy or minimality assumptions. An unused or zero-probability state is plainly unidentifiable, and the Gaussian-mixture argument requires active components. The two-case elbow experiment does not establish consistent recovery of K.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states needs justification: marginalizing a source state shared across all outgoing edges generally couples destination variables, while Equation 57 factorizes them. Likewise, p(s_t|x_t) is not generally the full posterior when s_t affects x_{t+1}.

Most causal baselines are stationary and therefore structurally disadvantaged. The directly relevant R-PCMCI baseline is evaluated only on the GRN task using default settings after tuning failures, while no meaningful baseline comparison is provided for recurrent conditional-graph recovery.

The empirical evidence lacks adequate uncertainty reporting, seed counts, and ablations. The GRN result uses one simulated topology, and its best F1 is only 0.347. NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth or interventions, gives only a small improvement over ACD, and therefore cannot validate the causal or interpretability claims. These issues, combined with the theoretical gap, make rejection more appropriate despite the promising idea.

strengths: The manuscript tackles an important and difficult setting: causal discovery when interactions vary with latent, variable-specific states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive, compact alternative to enumerating K^N global regimes. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-zf10698q/call-098f6c0341ce49e3b5b7bd64becb61b2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
SDCI combines amortized graph inference, discrete state modeling, and message-passing dynamics into a coherent framework covering observed, determined, and recurrent-state cases.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene networks, and real NBA trajectories. Results are promising, especially for determined states and DynGen graph recovery.

The paper is generally well organized, includes substantial implementation and dataset details, provides code, and candidly acknowledges difficulties with variational consistency and recurrent-state inference.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not established under the stated assumptions. Theorem A.6 applies finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise without requiring positive mixing weights or sufficient visitation of every regime. Because the state law is unrestricted—and determined states can produce zero-one conditional weights—unvisited regimes and their graphs are plainly unidentifiable. This also undermines the claims of requiring no assumptions on state dependence and identifying an unknown K.

Corollary A.8 contains a consequential invalid step: permutation invariance of an aggregator does not imply equal partial derivatives with respect to different messages evaluated at unequal inputs, much less across receivers. Moreover, equality of products involving derivatives of g and f_e does not separately identify f_e when g and its alternative parameterization may absorb transformations. Thus global edge-type-label identifiability is unsupported. The required derivative assumptions are also neither guaranteed nor verified for the implemented leaky-ReLU networks.

The claimed exact inference for determined states is not justified as written. Unless states are deterministic, the posterior of s_t given the full sequence includes the likelihood of future observations and is not simply p(s_t|x_t). Equation 57 also appears to replace a K^N mixture through a nonlinear decoder with independently marginalized messages; this is generally not an exact marginalization.

The empirical comparisons do not cleanly isolate the contribution. In the variable-graph experiment, SDCI learns shared dynamics from 10,000 sequences whereas Rhino and N-GC are retrained from individual sequences of length 80, and most baselines assume stationarity by construction. Relevant switching or state-conditioned alternatives, capacity-matched ablations, and ablations of the state and edge-type components are missing.

Statistical reporting is insufficient: the number of training seeds is unstated, several central results and the GRN table lack uncertainty, error bars are undefined, F1 threshold selection is unspecified, and label-permutation alignment is not described. The two-example elbow experiment is weak evidence for practical recovery of K.

The real-data evidence supports forecasting rather than causal discovery. NBA gains over ACD are small and shown without uncertainty or a matched noncausal latent-state model, while learned edges receive only qualitative interpretations. DynGen additionally uses simulated longitudinal measurements unavailable in ordinary single-cell experiments, so the claimed immediate biological applicability is overstated.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is a useful and intuitive representation that reduces the exponential regime-graph description to a compact set of source-state-dependent graphs.
SDCI is a well-motivated extension of amortized causal discovery and neural relational inference, combining discrete states, typed edges, and message passing in a coherent model.

The evaluation covers controlled physical simulations, a semi-synthetic gene-regulatory system, and real multi-agent trajectories. The paper also candidly reports poor performance in the harder recurrent, sample-varying setting.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams, substantial implementation detail, relevant recent citations, and publicly identified code.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not established under the stated assumptions. State dynamics are unrestricted and may be deterministic, yet no positivity, full-support, or state-visitation assumption ensures that all K^N mixture components occur. Zero-probability or unvisited regimes can be altered or added without changing p(x), so finite Gaussian-mixture identifiability cannot recover U, K, or those regimes' graphs. This directly undermines the claimed coverage of determined states and unknown K.

Corollary A.8 relies on an invalid step: permutation invariance of the aggregator does not imply equal partial derivatives across its inputs or targets; for example, a sum of squared messages is permutation invariant but has input-dependent derivatives. Equality of products involving aggregator and edge-function derivatives also does not force a single global permutation of edge types. Consequently, identifiability of W is unsupported under assumption (m5).

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is incorrect for the presented model. The posterior of s_t generally depends on x_{t+1} through the observation decoder, so q(s_t|x_t)=p_s(s_t|x_t) is not the exact posterior. Moreover, nonlinear aggregation and the fact that one source state affects multiple targets prevent the state sum from factorizing as asserted in Eq. (57).

There is a substantial theory-method mismatch: the proofs treat regime structures as model-level objects, whereas SDCI infers a latent, sample-specific W that is marginalized under a prior. Identifiability of the latter and consistency of the amortized estimator are not shown. The practical model also imposes locally factorized state dynamics, while the paper advertises unrestricted dependencies.

The empirical comparison does not isolate the main contribution. Most baselines assume stationarity and can output only an aggregate summary graph; no strong switching-graph baseline, oracle-state decomposition, or comparable two-stage method is evaluated on conditional-graph recovery. Performance for recurrent sample-specific graphs is weak even at small scale.

Statistical support is insufficient: several key figures and the GRN table omit numbers of runs and uncertainty; threshold selection and label-permutation matching are unspecified. The GRN result uses one semi-synthetic setting and reaches only 0.347 F1, while the NBA experiment has no causal ground truth and shows only a small, uncertainty-free forecasting advantage under differing architectures and training budgets.

The unknown-K evidence consists of two selected reconstruction-error curves using an informal elbow heuristic rather than the likelihood-based model-selection argument in the theory. This is not enough to support reliable recovery of K.

strengths: The paper addresses an important setting—causal discovery when interactions change with latent, potentially observation-dependent states—and motivates it clearly.
The conditional summary graph is a useful, interpretable factorization of an exponentially large regime graph into source-state-specific structures.
SDCI coherently combines latent-state modeling, amortized graph inference, and GNN interaction decoders, covering observed, determined, recurrent, fixed-graph, and sample-varying settings.
The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, a 49-gene semi-synthetic system, and NBA trajectories. The particle experiments show promising recovery under several configurations.

The presentation is generally readable, the appendix supplies substantial implementation detail, and the authors appropriately acknowledge that estimator consistency and recurrent-state inference remain open challenges.
weaknesses: Major theoretical issue: Theorem 4.3 is not established under the stated assumptions. Applying finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability in Eq. 35 requires active components with suitable positive weights. No assumption ensures that every state or joint state configuration occurs with positive probability on adequate support; determined states can even make the conditional weights zero or one. Unvisited regimes, their graphs, and K can therefore be changed without altering p(x). This directly undermines the claims of arbitrary state dependence and unknown-K identifiability.

Major proof error: Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across messages and receivers. This is false for a general permutation-invariant function—for example, a sum of squared messages—and even a sum-then-MLP generally has different derivatives at different receivers. Equality of products involving unknown g and edge functions does not isolate a single global edge-type permutation. Definition 4.1, Eq. 17, is also logically malformed as written.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is not justified. Unless states are explicitly deterministic, p(s_t|x_t) is not the posterior because s_t also affects x_{t+1}. Moreover, marginalizing categorical messages through a nonlinear Gaussian decoder produces a K^N-component mixture; Eq. 57 does not show that this can be reduced elementwise. The implemented leaky-ReLU networks also do not automatically satisfy the stated analytic/distinct-derivative assumptions.

The main baseline comparison on particles evaluates only the union summary graph, not the advertised conditional summary graphs or edge labels W. Most baselines are stationary methods; an appropriate latent switching baseline is not evaluated there. R-PCMCI appears only in the GRN experiment and is run with default settings after tuning attempts failed, limiting the strength of the superiority claim.

Experimental uncertainty is inadequately reported. Several central figures and the GRN table have no seed count, error bars, or significance tests; graph-threshold selection and latent-label permutation alignment are unspecified. The best GRN F1 is only 0.347, its AUROC differs from Rhino by 0.003, and the NBA forecasting curves are close, so variability could change the conclusions.

Unknown-K evidence consists of two reconstruction-error elbow plots rather than likelihood-based model selection or quantitative K-recovery experiments. NBA forecasting and qualitative learned graphs cannot validate causal discovery without causal ground truth, interventions, or downstream robustness tests.

Practical scope is limited by the acknowledged exponential recurrent-state inference: sample-varying recurrent recovery is already weak with three variables, the 49-gene experiment requires batch size one, and no runtime or memory analysis is provided. Thus the broad scalability claims are not yet convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored setting: lagged causal discovery when per-variable latent states change interactions over time. Its observed, determined, and recurrent state taxonomy makes the intended scope reasonably clear.

The conditional summary graph is a useful compact representation under the source-wise state factorization: K state-conditioned graphs replace K^N global regime graphs while retaining which source-state activates each edge.

SDCI is a natural extension of amortized relational discovery that jointly models graph labels and latent states. The synthetic experiments demonstrate strong recovery in favorable fixed-graph and determined-state settings.

The evaluation spans physical simulations, a semi-synthetic gene-regulatory system, and NBA trajectories. The appendix provides substantial architectural, training, and data-generation detail, together with a code link.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability claim is not established. Theorem A.6 invokes finite Gaussian-mixture identifiability without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. Unreachable regimes—and deterministic settings where only one component is active for a history—can have arbitrary graphs without changing the observed distribution. Consequently, recovery of all regimes and of U or K does not follow under the advertised unrestricted state dynamics.

Corollary A.8 has a separate major gap. Equality of products involving derivatives of g and f_e does not identify the edge type when both functions are unknown. Moreover, permutation invariance does not imply equal partial derivatives across targets, or even across inputs for a general symmetric aggregator. A non-injective symmetric aggregator can make distinct edge functions observationally equivalent while satisfying the stated derivative assumptions, invalidating Theorem 4.3 without substantially stronger conditions.

The connection between theory and implementation is weak. Generic GNN/MLP parameterizations do not guarantee the required nonzero derivatives or edge-type separation; the employed leaky-ReLU functions are not analytic. Estimator consistency is explicitly unresolved. The claimed exact determined-state marginalization also appears to ignore that a source state jointly couples messages to every target and that nonlinear decoding generally cannot be interchanged with elementwise state marginalization.

The empirical causal-discovery evidence is insufficient to compensate for these theoretical problems. Key results lack repeated-run uncertainty and seed information, variable-graph recurrent recovery deteriorates substantially, and unknown-K selection is supported only by two subjective reconstruction-error elbow plots rather than a validated selection procedure.

Baseline comparisons are not fully persuasive: SDCI uses 10,000 simulated training sequences while Rhino and N-GC are retrained from individual short trajectories, close switching approaches receive little evaluation, and R-PCMCI is left at default settings after tuning failures. Evaluating only union summary graphs also does not directly validate the claimed conditional graphs.

The GRN study uses one simulator configuration with artificially longitudinal single-cell traces, reports a low best F1 of 0.347 without AUPRC, threshold analysis, or uncertainty, and therefore does not support broad biological claims. The NBA experiment has no causal ground truth; its advantage over ACD is slight and unquantified, while the graph interpretations could reflect position clustering rather than recovered causal structure.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pzx2_hk8/call-0474d8950f334fcd861d27287fef0c6c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem. Its conditional summary graph is an intuitive, compact alternative to enumerating K^N global regimes.
SDCI is a coherent synthesis of discrete latent-state inference, amortized graph inference, and GNN dynamics, covering observed, observation-determined, and recurrent states.

The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories. Results are promising for fixed-graph and determined-state settings, and SDCI obtains the best reported GRN F1 score.
The paper discusses relevant recent work, states many modeling assumptions explicitly, provides extensive implementation details, and links to code.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not convincingly established. Theorem A.6 invokes finite Gaussian-mixture identifiability as if every regime had positive conditional weight for almost every history. No positivity, reachability, or minimal-mixture assumption is imposed; indeed, when states are determined by observations, only one regime may have nonzero probability at a fixed conditioning value. Equation (36) therefore does not follow for every regime, and unused regimes can be changed or added without affecting the observed distribution. This undermines both the claimed unrestricted state dependence and identification of unknown K.

Corollary A.8 contains another material proof gap: permutation invariance of g does not imply that its partial derivatives with respect to different messages are equal (for example, a symmetric sum of squared messages has unequal partial derivatives at unequal inputs). Assumption (a2) only distinguishes functions within a model and does not justify the asserted global alignment of edge-type labels across observationally equivalent decompositions. Definition 4.1's zero-edge equivalence is also formally inconsistent as written.

The theory does not establish consistency of the proposed variational estimator, which the paper acknowledges remains open. Moreover, the implemented leaky-ReLU networks do not satisfy the stated analytic-function rationale. The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is questionable: marginalizing discrete messages before a nonlinear aggregator is generally not equivalent to summing over the K^N state configurations, and p(s_t|x_t) is not the full posterior when future observations depend on s_t.

The empirical comparisons do not directly validate the main state-dependent causal-discovery claim. Most baselines are evaluated only on the union summary graph, the recurrent synthetic setting lacks a competitive regime-switching baseline, the GRN conditional graphs are assessed mainly qualitatively, and NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth. Predictive improvement alone is not evidence that the learned edges are causal.

Most key results lack repeated-run uncertainty, significance analysis, and adequate reporting of thresholding or permutation alignment for F1. The K-selection claim rests on only two illustrative reconstruction-error curves, while R-PCMCI is evaluated with defaults after tuning failures. Performance also degrades substantially for variable recurrent graphs, with no runtime or scaling study.

The claimed scope is broader than the actual model: it excludes hidden confounding and instantaneous effects, assumes first-order Gaussian additive-noise dynamics and source-local state gating, and factorizes state evolution across variables. This does not cover motivating cases where one agent's state depends on other agents' histories. In addition, identifiability only up to separate state permutations for every source does not identify globally aligned conditional regimes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: causal discovery when lagged interactions change with latent, variable-specific states. This is a useful extension beyond stationary or single-global-regime formulations.

The conditional summary graph is intuitive and compact under the stated row-wise state model, reducing a K^N collection of regime graphs to K state-conditioned graphs. The graphical exposition and GNN-based realization are generally clear.

The evaluation spans controlled particle systems, a 49-gene DynGen simulation, and NBA trajectories. SDCI shows promising summary-graph and GRN F1 results, including settings where graph structures vary across samples.

Implementation details, hyperparameters, data-generation procedures, and a code repository are provided, and the paper appropriately acknowledges limitations involving estimator consistency, recurrent-state inference, and practical selection of K.
weaknesses: The central identifiability argument omits necessary state-support assumptions. Applying finite Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise requires all claimed regimes to have positive conditional weights, whereas the allowed state dynamics include deterministic states, zero-probability regimes, and unreachable configurations. Such regimes and their graphs cannot be identified, undermining Theorems A.6-A.7 and the claims of unrestricted state dependence and unknown-K recovery.

Corollary A.8 does not convincingly establish identifiability of edge-type labels. Equality of products involving derivatives of two different aggregators and edge functions does not identify the edge-function labels; assumption (a2) only separates functions within each model. Moreover, permutation invariance does not imply equal derivatives across unequal messages or target variables. The assertion that analytic functions guarantee (a2.2) is also false in general, and the implemented leaky-ReLU networks are not analytic.

The claimed O(NK) exact inference for determined states is unsupported. The posterior of s_t generally also depends on x_{t+1} and W, while the nonlinear decoder couples all source states. Equation (57) leaves the messages unintegrated and does not justify element-wise marginalization, so setting q(s_t|x_t)=p(s_t|x_t) is not generally exact.

There is a substantial theory-algorithm gap: the proofs effectively concern a fixed conditional graph, while SDCI samples W per sequence and infers it from a single finite trajectory. Identifiability or consistency for this latent-W, amortized setting is not established. The remaining assumptions—first-order dynamics, Gaussian additive noise, no instantaneous effects or hidden confounding, faithfulness, and distinct outgoing support for every state—are also restrictive and are not empirically stress-tested.

Empirical reliability is difficult to assess because the paper reports no number of training seeds, uncertainty across runs, statistical tests, or definitions for several error bars. F1 threshold selection is unspecified, ablations are absent, the GRN study uses one simulated setup, and R-PCMCI is evaluated with defaults after tuning failures. Comparisons to other recent regime-dependent causal-discovery methods are missing.

The unknown-K evidence consists of two test-reconstruction elbow plots, which neither validate likelihood-based model selection nor demonstrate reliable K recovery. On NBA data the forecasting advantage over ACD is small, there is no causal ground truth, the game-level train/test split is unspecified, and the causal interpretations are therefore largely qualitative.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-fl0q_0hy/call-e503aa5b3178439aa8cc8c89e21481ab/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important setting: nonstationary time-series causal discovery with local latent states. Conditional summary graphs provide a compact and interpretable alternative to enumerating exponentially many global regimes.

SDCI is a coherent combination of amortized graph inference, discrete latent-state modeling, and GNN dynamics, accommodating observed, observation-determined, and recurrent states as well as sample-specific structures.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks, and NBA trajectories. Several results are promising, including strong synthetic recovery and a DynGen F1 score of 0.347 versus 0.187 for the strongest reported baseline.

The assumptions, architecture, optimization details, and datasets are documented extensively, code is provided, and the authors candidly acknowledge consistency, recurrent-state complexity, and practical selection of the number of states as open challenges.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability result appears false as stated. Theorem A.6 applies finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability to Eq. 35 without assuming positive mixture weights or adequate state support. Under the claimed unrestricted state dynamics, a regime may never occur; in the determined case, conditional weights can be zero or one on disjoint regions. Unused regime graphs and even K can then be changed without altering the observed distribution, directly contradicting the claimed graph and unknown-K identifiability.

The proof of conditional-effect-label identifiability has another substantive gap. Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across inputs; this is generally false for symmetric nonlinear functions because derivatives depend on the individual message values. Moreover, the unknown aggregators can absorb reparameterizations of the edge functions. Assumptions (a2.1-a2.2) therefore do not establish the required single global permutation of edge types. The accompanying claim that analyticity guarantees (a2.2) is also incorrect in general.

The experiments do not directly validate the central target broadly enough. Baseline comparisons usually collapse conditional summary graphs into their union and are largely restricted to determined-state data, so they do not assess regime-resolved recovery. Comparisons with stronger switching or oracle-state methods and ablations isolating state inference, conditional edges, and amortization are missing.

The variable-graph comparison is difficult to interpret fairly: SDCI shares statistical strength across 10,000 training sequences, whereas Rhino and N-GC are retrained on individual length-80 sequences. Many headline plots and the single DynGen configuration lack seed-level uncertainties or statistical tests, and the reported model-selection evidence consists of only two favorable synthetic curves.

The biological and real-data conclusions are overstated. DynGen is semi-synthetic and assumes longitudinal measurements of the same cells, while the NBA data provide neither causal ground truth nor interventional validation. The NBA forecasting improvement over ACD is slight, and hand-designed or spatially partitioned states plus qualitative graph visualizations cannot demonstrate causal discovery.

Recurrent-state inference retains exponential complexity and visibly degrades as the problem grows. The claimed exact marginalization for determined states is insufficiently justified when nonlinear aggregation couples messages, and practical recovery of K remains heuristic. These limitations materially narrow the method's usable regime.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: causal discovery when interactions change with latent, observation-dependent states. The observed/determined/recurrent taxonomy clearly motivates the intended scope.

The conditional summary graph is an intuitive and potentially useful representation. Under the source-local state assumption, it compresses K^N global regimes into K state-indexed graphs while retaining more information than an ordinary summary graph.

SDCI is a coherent combination of amortized graph inference, discrete latent-state modeling, and message passing. It accommodates both shared and sample-specific structures and provides interpretable state-conditioned edge labels.

The evaluation spans controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene networks, and real player trajectories. Results for determined states and the DynGen F1 score are promising, even though they do not fully establish the causal claims.

The exposition and diagrams are generally clear, and the appendices provide architecture, training, and dataset details together with a code link. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-vpkljkio/call-58277235befd4e34be69407d4184c8a2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Major: The main identifiability theorem is not established. The proof applies ordinary finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise after conditioning on history, but it assumes neither positive mixture weights nor reachability of all K^N state configurations. Determined states can produce zero/one weights, and unused regimes immediately make U and K unidentifiable. Moreover, pointwise mixture identification only supplies a permutation depending on the covariate and history; the argument that this becomes one global permutation is unsupported.

Major: Corollary A.8 contains an invalid inference. Equality of products involving derivatives of the aggregator and message functions does not identify the message-function label because the aggregator derivatives can differ between models. Permutation invariance makes an aggregator symmetric, but does not make its partial derivatives equal when evaluated at different messages. Consequently, the claimed global permutation of edge types does not follow. Definition 4.1/Eq. 17 is also internally inconsistent as written, and W includes diagonal labels that never enter the i≠j decoder.

Major: The claimed exact inference for determined states is generally incorrect. Equations 57–58 move marginalization through a nonlinear aggregation function and Gaussian likelihood; the likelihood couples all source states, so summing individual state/message marginals is not equivalent to summing over joint configurations or evaluating the decoder at expected messages. Likewise, p(s_t|x_t) is not generally the posterior given the full sequence because x_{t+1} depends on s_t. The method may still be a useful approximation, but the derivation and claims must be revised.

The experiments do not adequately test the central conditional-graph contribution against appropriate alternatives. The main cross-method particle comparison unions conditional graphs into ordinary summary graphs, discarding precisely the state-conditioned information SDCI is designed to recover. Regime-aware R-PCMCI is used only in the GRN experiment under acknowledged implementation difficulties, and recovery with recurrent, sample-varying graphs remains weak.

The empirical reporting is insufficient for firm conclusions: random-seed counts and uncertainty are absent from most results; exact numerical values, threshold selection, and permutation alignment for latent-state/edge F1 are unspecified; and there are no focused ablations. Baseline treatment is uneven, including a much smaller Rhino network and essentially untuned R-PCMCI. Rhino's AUROC of 0.933 versus SDCI's 0.936 but F1 of 0.081 versus 0.347 especially calls for AUPRC and a common threshold-selection protocol.

The broader claims exceed the evidence. DynGen provides only one semi-synthetic configuration and relies on longitudinal measurements unavailable in the motivating single-cell setting. NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth, shows only a small advantage over ACD/NRI without uncertainty, and cannot validate the learned edges as causal; the qualitative interpretations are post hoc. The two reconstruction-error curves for selecting K also do not demonstrate identifiability or reliable model selection. These empirical results do not compensate for the failures in the principal theoretical claims.
