strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and introduces an intuitive factorization of exponentially many joint regimes into state-indexed outgoing structures. The conditional summary graph is a potentially useful representation. This assessment is based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-l5pqw_dv/call-57455e73e0f240d493cc5debba337770/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

SDCI is a coherent extension of amortized relational inference, integrating discrete local states, edge types, and a graph-network decoder. Considering observed, observation-determined, and recurrent states within one framework is practically appealing.

The evaluation spans controlled particle dynamics, semi-synthetic gene regulation, and real player trajectories. Results include nearly perfect edge recovery in the fixed-graph particle setting, improved summary-graph scores over stationary baselines, and the best reported DynGen F1 score.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear, surveys relevant nonstationary causal-discovery literature, supplies substantial implementation and dataset details, links code, and appropriately acknowledges that consistency of the variational estimator remains open.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not established. Theorem A.6 invokes finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability at each conditioned history to conclude that all U regimes—and hence U—are identifiable, but no positivity or visitation assumption is imposed on the history-dependent mixture weights. In the paper's determined-state setting, the state posterior at a fixed history is a point mass, so only one component is present. More generally, never-visited regimes with distinct graphs can be added without changing the observational distribution. This directly undermines the advertised guarantees for arbitrary state dependencies and unknown K.

Corollary A.8 contains another substantive gap. Permutation invariance of g does not imply that its partial derivatives with respect to different messages or targets are equal at arbitrary inputs. Moreover, equality of products involving derivatives of g and the edge functions does not identify edge-type labels when both function classes can be reparameterized. Consequently, the claimed single global permutation of nonzero edge types does not follow. The actual leaky-ReLU networks also do not satisfy the suggested analyticity argument, while assumptions (a1) and (a2) are neither enforced nor empirically checked.

The claimed O(NK) exact marginalization for determined states in Appendix B.2 is generally invalid. The nonlinear aggregator and Gaussian output likelihood couple all incoming messages, so independently marginalizing each state and then evaluating the decoder is not equivalent to summing the likelihood over K^N joint state configurations without additional linearity assumptions.

The experiments do not provide a direct competitive validation of the main conditional-graph contribution. Figures 4–5 evaluate SDCI's conditional labels without baselines, whereas Figure 6 compares only the union summary graph, discarding state dependence. The closest switching-regime baseline is omitted from the controlled particle study and is run with defaults on DynGen after tuning reportedly produced errors.

Some comparisons are materially asymmetric. In the variable-graph setting, SDCI learns shared dynamics from 10,000 training sequences, while Rhino and N-GC are retrained from each short test sequence. The paper also does not specify seed counts, define several error bars, explain permutation alignment for state/edge-label F1, or document threshold selection. The large AUROC/F1 discrepancies in Table 1 make the missing threshold protocol especially consequential.

The application evidence is insufficient for the causal and practical claims. DynGen supplies only semi-synthetic longitudinal trajectories unavailable in ordinary single-cell experiments, achieves a modest best F1 of 0.347, and has no uncertainty estimates. NBA has neither causal nor state ground truth; SDCI's forecasting difference from ACD is very small and unquantified, while the learned-graph interpretations are qualitative and post hoc. Forecasting improvements over differently trained architectures do not validate causal discovery.

The broad framing is at odds with strong restrictions: first-order lagged dynamics, no instantaneous effects or hidden confounding, independent homoscedastic Gaussian noise, shared edge-function types, and a distinct outgoing adjacency for every local state. The two-example reconstruction-error elbow experiment is also inadequate support for reliable recovery of K. Because these issues affect the principal theoretical and empirical conclusions rather than being minor correctable omissions, acceptance is not currently justified.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: causal discovery when interactions vary according to latent, node-specific states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive representation that compresses K^N global regimes into state-conditioned outgoing-edge structures. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8up8igaj/call-80017f6d68344bc6a82f91470dd1daa1/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

SDCI is a well-motivated extension of amortized causal discovery, combining per-node latent states, discrete edge types, and a GNN dynamics model. Treating observed, observation-determined, and recurrent states in one framework is useful.

The evaluation covers controlled physical systems, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories, including fixed and sample-varying graphs, different numbers of variables and states, and a preliminary model-selection experiment. Several results are promising, particularly fixed-graph recovery and the DynGen F1 score.

The paper discusses relevant recent literature, acknowledges that consistency of the variational estimator remains open, provides substantial implementation and data-generation detail, and links to code.
weaknesses: The central identifiability guarantee is not convincingly established. Definition 4.1/A.3 is itself inconsistent: Eq. 17 states equality of the two numerical labels iff the first label is zero, which conflicts with Eq. 18 whenever a nonzero label is unchanged by the permutation. More substantively, Theorem A.6 invokes finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise without requiring positive probability for every regime. The unrestricted state law permits unused states, while observation-determined states can give 0/1 conditional mixture weights; in either case U and hence K cannot be identified as claimed. The argument converting an input-dependent component permutation into a global permutation is also asserted rather than proved.

Corollary A.8 contains another consequential gap. Equality of products involving derivatives of g and the edge functions does not identify the individual edge-function labels when both functions may change between observationally equivalent models. Moreover, permutation invariance of g does not imply that its partial derivatives are equal across inputs or targets (for example, a symmetric sum of squared messages has unequal derivatives). Thus the claimed global edge-type permutation does not follow from assumptions (a1-a2). The result also identifies outgoing structures only up to separate permutations for every source node, which does not identify the globally indexed graphs G_k up to one common state permutation.

The claimed O(NK) exact inference for determined states in Eqs. 57-58 is generally invalid. Because the nonlinear aggregator and Gaussian likelihood jointly couple all incoming messages, marginalizing independent node states yields a sum over K^N state configurations; it cannot generally be factorized into independent edge-wise sums or replaced by evaluation at averaged messages. Likewise, setting the generative state conditional q_s=p_s is not generally the posterior once future observations depend on the state. This affects both the methodological interpretation and computational claims.

The experiments do not directly validate the main conditional-structure claim against competitive alternatives. On particles, baselines are evaluated only on the union summary graph, rather than W or the conditional graphs, and mostly only for determined states. For sample-varying graphs, Rhino and N-GC are fitted separately to each length-80 sample, whereas SDCI amortizes learning over 10,000 samples with shared dynamics; this comparison confounds the proposed nonstationary mechanism with access to pooled training data.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for the strength of the empirical claims: the number of training runs, random seeds, interpretation of error bars, variability for Table 1, F1 threshold selection, and label-permutation alignment are not reported. Sparse GRNs warrant AUPRC as well as AUROC, and the K-selection claim is supported by only two visually inspected elbow curves without a quantitative selection rule or success rate.

The application conclusions are overstated. DynGen is a single semi-synthetic configuration rather than real biological validation, and SDCI's best AUROC is essentially tied with Rhino while the large F1 difference may depend on unspecified thresholding. NBA forecasting has no causal or state ground truth, shows only a small unquantified improvement, and likely violates the no-confounding and first-order assumptions; consequently, anecdotal graph visualizations cannot establish causal interpretability. The practical state model is also factorized by node and the experiments largely use states determined by each node's own measurements, so the advertised breadth of arbitrary feedback-dependent states is not empirically tested.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is an intuitive and potentially useful representation: under the paper’s source-specific state model, it reduces K^N joint regimes to K state-indexed graphs while retaining state-dependent interactions.

SDCI provides a coherent combination of latent-state inference, amortized graph discovery, and graph-neural dynamics, covering observed, determined, and recurrent state settings as well as sample-specific graphs.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories. Results show strong synthetic recovery and encouraging GRN gains, particularly an F1 score of 0.347 versus 0.187 for the strongest reported baseline.

The relationship to recent nonstationary causal-discovery work is discussed thoughtfully, and substantial architectural, training, and data-generation details are supplied alongside public code. The reviewed manuscript is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-cuecmqhk/call-dc6ffed5df9a40799e88efbea78df51e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not convincingly established under the stated assumptions. Theorem A.6 invokes finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability for p(x_t|x_{1:t-1}) without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. With arbitrary determined or recurrent state dependencies, configurations can be impossible or have zero weight, so their graphs and even K are unidentifiable. The subsequent claim that history-dependent component matchings reduce to one global permutation also needs stronger support and regularity conditions than the proof supplies.

Corollary A.8 relies on an invalid implication: permutation invariance of the aggregator does not make its partial derivatives equal for unequal messages or across targets. Moreover, equality of products involving separately learned aggregators and interaction functions does not by itself identify global edge-type labels. The claims that the implemented GNN automatically satisfies (a2.1) and that analyticity guarantees (a2.2) are also unjustified; the actual decoder uses non-analytic leaky-ReLU networks. Thus identifiability of W, rather than merely edge support, remains doubtful.

Appendix B.2 calls determined-state inference exact and O(NK), but the independent state sums remain coupled through the nonlinear aggregator and Gaussian likelihood. Replacing messages by the expression in Eq. 16 is generally a sampling or soft relaxation, not exact marginalization. This creates a significant mismatch between the probabilistic derivation and implementation.

The experiments do not decisively validate the main conditional causal object. Most baseline comparisons score only the union summary graph; there is no oracle-state ablation, comparably expressive switching noncausal model, or regime-dependent baseline on the main synthetic benchmark. NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth, so predictive gains and qualitative edge visualizations cannot establish causal discovery.

Statistical reporting is incomplete: the number of runs, random seeds, meanings of error bars, graph-threshold selection, and variability for Table 1 are unspecified. The claim that K can be selected is illustrated by only two reconstruction curves whose elbows are not unequivocally at the true K. The GRN study also uses one simulator configuration and longitudinal measurements of the same simulated cell, limiting its support for realistic single-cell applications.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and insufficiently studied setting: causal structures that vary with latent, variable-specific states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive, compact alternative to enumerating exponentially many joint regimes.

SDCI is a technically interesting extension of amortized relational inference, combining discrete state inference, state-conditioned edge types, and graph-neural dynamics for observed, determined, and recurrent-state settings.

The experiments are reasonably broad. SDCI performs strongly on the controlled physics data, obtains the best F1 score on the DynGen network, and gives encouraging forecasting results on NBA trajectories.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes extensive derivations, architectural and training details, dataset descriptions, and a code reference.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability claim does not follow under the stated assumptions. Applying finite-mixture identifiability requires every regime to have positive conditional mixing weight, but no state-support assumption is imposed. A state configuration can have zero probability—particularly naturally in the determined-state setting—while its graph is changed arbitrarily without affecting the observed distribution. This directly contradicts Theorems A.6–A.8 and weakens the claim that K is identifiable without assumptions on state dynamics.

The proof of conditional edge-type identifiability contains another substantive gap: it asserts that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across different message arguments. This is false for general permutation-invariant functions. Moreover, analyticity alone does not guarantee assumption (a2.2), and the learned MLP/GNN implementation is not shown to satisfy either functional condition. Consequently, the theorem is not established for the proposed model even after adding a state-support condition.

The empirical causal evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous to compensate for the theoretical problems. Several central plots lack uncertainty estimates and the number of training seeds is unspecified. Most baselines assume stationarity and cannot estimate the proposed conditional graph, while the closest regime-dependent baseline is not evaluated on the main physics experiments. Thus the comparisons do not isolate the benefit of SDCI's particular state-dependent construction.

The real-world conclusions are overstated. The GRN study uses one semi-synthetic DynGen configuration and longitudinal measurements of the same simulated cells, which are unavailable in ordinary single-cell experiments. NBA has no causal ground truth; its learned graphs receive only qualitative, post-hoc interpretations, and the small forecasting differences from ACD are reported without significance estimates.

The claimed scope is broader than the actual assumptions: no latent confounding or instantaneous effects, first-order homoscedastic Gaussian dynamics, distinct outgoing topology for every state of every variable, and autonomous per-variable state transitions. The latter does not represent motivating examples in which one agent's state depends on other agents' histories. These restrictions and the acknowledged lack of consistency for per-sample graph inference should be reflected more clearly in the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored setting: causal discovery when interactions change according to local latent states. The observed/determined/recurrent taxonomy makes the problem easy to understand and motivates the proposed model well.
The conditional summary graph is a useful representation, reducing K^N global regimes to K state-indexed graphs while retaining which source-node state controls each interaction.

SDCI is a coherent combination of amortized graph inference, discrete state modeling, and message passing. It accommodates sample-specific structures and several state-observability settings within one framework.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled particle systems, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories. Results show strong synthetic recovery in favorable settings and a meaningful GRN F1 improvement over the reported baselines.

The manuscript is polished and generally self-contained, with extensive implementation and dataset details, code availability, and unusually candid discussion of limitations such as variational consistency and recurrent-state complexity.
weaknesses: The central identifiability result is not established under the stated assumptions. The Gaussian-mixture argument in Theorem A.6 requires every regime to have positive conditional weight, but no support or reachability assumption is imposed. In the paper's determined-state setting, states can be deterministic functions of observations, so all but one mixture weight are zero at a given input; unused regimes and their graphs can then be changed without altering the observational distribution. This directly undermines the claims of identifiability without assumptions on state dynamics and of identifying K.

The proof of conditional-effect label identifiability contains another substantial gap. It argues that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across inputs and destinations, which is false for a general permutation-invariant function—for example, a symmetric sum of squared messages has different derivatives at different messages. Moreover, equality of products involving unknown aggregator and edge-function derivatives does not by itself identify edge types across two models. Thus Corollary A.8 needs materially stronger assumptions or a different proof.

The connection between theory and the implemented estimator is incomplete. The theory effectively concerns population distributions with fixed mechanisms, whereas SDCI infers a new W from one finite trajectory per sample; identifiability of these sample-specific graphs is not shown. The claim of exact state inference in the determined case is also questionable: setting q(s_t|x) equal to the state prior ignores information about s_t contained in x_{t+1}, and averaging or sampling state-dependent messages is not generally equivalent to exactly marginalizing the resulting mixture likelihood.

The causal-discovery experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. On the particle data, competing stationary methods are evaluated only on the union summary graph, while relevant switching/regime-dependent methods are not compared on recovery of the proposed conditional graph. R-PCMCI appears only in the GRN experiment and is run with default settings after tuning failures. Ablations, compute comparisons, clearly defined repeated training seeds, and uncertainty for most reported results are missing.

The real-data evidence does not validate causal recovery. The GRN study uses a simulator, obtains a best F1 of only 0.347, and reports no repeated simulations or precision-recall metric despite severe sparsity. NBA has no causal ground truth; its small forecasting advantage and qualitative graphs could arise from additional latent-state capacity rather than causal correctness, so claims about causality-driven forecasting and interpretability are too strong.

Selection of K is demonstrated only through an informal elbow in test reconstruction error on two synthetic examples, without a validation criterion, likelihood-based comparison, or recovery frequency across runs. Together with the sharp degradation in the recurrent and variable-graph settings, this leaves practical model selection and scalability unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: causal discovery when temporal interactions change according to latent, potentially recurrent states.
The conditional summary graph is an intuitive compact representation, and the source-specific state factorization avoids explicitly parameterizing all K^N global regimes.
SDCI combines latent-state modeling, amortized graph inference, and GNN dynamics coherently. The determined, recurrent, and observed-state variants cover several useful settings.

The evaluation spans controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene networks, and NBA trajectories. Several results—especially determined-state structure recovery and GRN F1—are promising, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail and a code link.
weaknesses: The central identifiability claim is not established under the stated assumptions. Theorem A.6 applies finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise in the history and concludes that all U components are identifiable, but it never requires every regime to have positive conditional probability. In the paper's determined-state setting, the conditional state distribution may be a point mass, leaving the other components unobservable. Consequently, the claims of identifiability without assumptions on state dependence and recovery of unknown K do not follow.

The proof of edge-type identifiability contains another serious gap. Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of the aggregator makes its partial derivatives equal across sources and targets; permutation invariance does not imply this, since derivatives generally depend on the message values and target inputs. Equality of the composite derivatives therefore cannot force a single global edge-type permutation. Definition A.3/Eq. 27 also appears logically malformed for nonzero labels.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is unconvincing. Equation 57 leaves latent messages effectively unmarginalized; passing independently marginalized state-conditioned messages through a nonlinear aggregator generally produces an exponential mixture, not the stated product. Moreover, q(s_t|x)=p(s_t|x_t) is not the posterior when s_t influences x_{t+1}, unless the state is strictly deterministic. This weakens the connection between the proposed objective and the probabilistic model.

The experiments do not directly benchmark the core state-conditioned graph target. Only SDCI is evaluated on W and latent-state recovery, while competing methods are reduced to an ordinary union summary graph. In the variable-graph experiment, SDCI also learns from 10,000 sequences whereas Rhino and N-GC are retrained on individual length-80 sequences. Oracle-state, regime-aware, or comparably amortized baselines are needed to isolate the contribution.

Empirical reporting is insufficiently rigorous: seeds and the meaning of error bars are unspecified, several principal results have no uncertainty, and there are no statistical tests. The two reconstruction-error curves do not demonstrate recovery of K because every over-specified value lies on essentially the same plateau. Important ablations for state inference, misspecified K, structural assumptions, runtime, and memory are absent.

The real-world evidence does not substantiate causal discovery. The GRN study uses one simulator and artificial same-cell longitudinal measurements, with best F1 only 0.347. NBA has no causal ground truth and provides only a small forecasting improvement plus qualitative dense graphs, in a domain likely violating the no-confounding and no-instantaneous-effect assumptions.

The theoretical setting remains restrictive—first-order Gaussian ANMs, no hidden confounders, unique outgoing adjacency for every local state, globally shared effect functions, and strong derivative conditions. The paper does not show that its generated data or leaky-ReLU implementation satisfy these conditions. Recurrent inference is acknowledged to scale exponentially, yet no scalability analysis is supplied. These issues make the broad practical and theoretical conclusions substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is an intuitive, useful representation that replaces K^N global regimes with K node-state-indexed graphs, addressing an important nonstationary causal-discovery setting. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-u0euds4e/call-0d736e8fc20a4004a67387b8dab5ea11/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
SDCI coherently combines latent state inference, typed interactions, and graph-neural dynamics, covering observed, determined, and recurrent states as well as sample-varying structures.

The controlled physical experiments show strong recovery in favorable fixed-graph and determined-state settings, while the simulated biological and real trajectory studies demonstrate potentially useful applications.

The paper is generally readable, discusses relevant recent work, supplies extensive implementation and dataset details, links code, and explicitly acknowledges that estimator consistency remains unresolved.
weaknesses: Major theoretical flaw: Theorem A.6 invokes finite-mixture identifiability pointwise without requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. In the emphasized determined-state case, the weights are typically 0/1; an unused regime can have an arbitrary graph, and zero-weight regimes can be added without changing p(x). Consequently, A.6 and downstream A.7-A.8 do not establish graph or unknown-K identifiability under the claimed unrestricted state dependencies.

Major theoretical flaw: Corollary A.8 incorrectly asserts that permutation invariance of g makes its coordinate derivatives equal. For example, g({h_i})=sum_i h_i^2 is permutation invariant but has coordinate-dependent derivatives; edge functions f and -f then satisfy the stated derivative-separation condition while producing identical dynamics after squaring. Edge labels may therefore change edgewise without a single global permutation, invalidating the principal conditional-effect identifiability claim. The statement that analyticity guarantees assumption (a2.2) is also false.

The claimed exact inference for determined states is not justified. Unless p(s_t|x_t) is a deterministic point mass, the posterior over s_t also depends on x_{t+1} through the state-dependent transition. Equation 57 does not actually integrate the latent messages and effectively exchanges marginalization with a nonlinear decoder, so the asserted O(NK) exact computation and resulting objective interpretation are unsound.

Even a repaired population identifiability theorem would concern fixed component mechanisms, whereas SDCI draws W anew for each sample and infers it from one finite trajectory. No result connects population mixture identifiability to recovery of these sample-specific graphs; the admitted lack of consistency theory is therefore directly relevant to the main algorithmic claim.

The empirical comparisons do not convincingly test the main output. On the physical data, baselines are compared only after SDCI's conditional graphs are collapsed into a union summary graph. There is no strong apples-to-apples conditional/regime-graph comparison, no matched-capacity ablation establishing that gains come from causal structure rather than extra latent-state capacity, and R-PCMCI is run with defaults after tuning attempts failed.

Evidence for broad superiority is weak: the number of independent runs and meaning of error bars are unspecified; the GRN study uses one simulated configuration and yields only 0.936 versus Rhino's 0.933 AUROC for the best SDCI variant, with other variants worse; and the NBA gain over ACD is small, lacks uncertainty, and has no causal ground truth. The qualitative NBA edge interpretations cannot validate causality under evidently questionable no-confounding and no-instantaneous-effect assumptions.

Unknown-K recovery is supported only by visually applying an elbow heuristic to test reconstruction MSE in two synthetic examples, rather than by likelihood-based selection, automatic recovery rates, or robustness analysis. This does not substantiate the advertised practical advantage.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: discovering time-varying causal structure when latent, variable-specific states modulate interactions. The conditional summary graph is a useful compact representation compared with enumerating K^N global regimes.

SDCI is a coherent synthesis of switching latent-variable models, amortized graph inference, and interaction-network decoders. The experiments span controlled physical data, a biological simulator, and multi-agent trajectories, and the paper candidly shows poor recovery in the difficult recurrent, variable-graph setting.

The presentation is generally readable and includes architectural, training, and dataset details plus a code link. The full manuscript and appendices were reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-21gct1z6/call-d0605479e9ec4040ad51f5b8e03333eb/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The main identifiability claim is not established for the advertised arbitrary state dependencies. Theorem A.6 applies finite-mixture identifiability to a K^N-component conditional Gaussian mixture without assuming positive probability or adequate support for every state configuration. In the determined-state case, the mixing distribution can be a point mass at each history; unused components, their graphs, and even K can then be changed without affecting p(x_1:T). This directly invalidates the claimed coverage of determined states and identification of an unknown K.

The proof of conditional-effect label identifiability has another major gap. Equation 47 equates products involving derivatives of both the interaction functions and the unknown aggregator. Within-model distinctness of the interaction derivatives does not force a cross-model global label permutation because changes can be absorbed by the aggregator. Moreover, permutation invariance does not imply equal partial derivatives across message arguments—e.g., a symmetric sum of squared messages has different derivatives at different messages—and certainly not across targets. The learned leaky-ReLU networks also do not enforce the stated analytic/distinctness conditions.

The claimed exact inference for determined states is incorrect. Since s_t controls x_{t+1}, the posterior of s_t given the sequence generally depends on x_{t+1}; it is not simply p_psi(s_t|x_t). Equations 57 and 16 effectively pass averaged or soft messages through a nonlinear decoder, which is not equivalent to marginalizing a mixture of nonlinear likelihoods. Consequently, the relationship between the implemented loss and the stated ELBO is unclear.

The scope is considerably narrower than suggested. An edge may depend only on the source variable's state, not the target state or a joint state; the model also excludes hidden confounding and instantaneous effects and assumes first-order Markov dynamics, Gaussian noise, shared interaction types, and a restrictive aggregation form. The paper explicitly leaves consistency of the variational estimator open, so even a corrected population identifiability result would not justify recovery by SDCI.

The evaluation does not convincingly test the central setting. The principal baseline comparison is restricted to determined-state synthetic data and evaluates only the union summary graph, discarding the conditional structure that is the proposed contribution. The recurrent, variable-graph case performs poorly even for few variables and receives no meaningful switching-model comparison. State and edge labels are identifiable only up to permutations, but the paper does not explain how labels are aligned before computing macro F1.

Experimental reliability and fairness are insufficiently documented: most results lack numerical tables, seed counts, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests; there is no ablation separating state modeling from additional capacity; and baseline tuning is asymmetric, including a 15-unit Rhino model versus 256-dimensional SDCI components and default/error-constrained configurations for other methods.

The unknown-K evidence is only an informal reconstruction-MSE elbow on two selected synthetic cases. It neither optimizes the claimed likelihood criterion nor measures how often K is recovered, and the plateaus are subjective. It cannot support practical or theoretical identification of K.

The application claims are overstated. The GRN study uses one semi-synthetic configuration, achieves only 0.347 best F1, and is not uniformly superior across variants and metrics. NBA has no causal ground truth; its states are handcrafted or learned directly from position, its inferred graphs are dense and interpreted post hoc, and the forecasting advantage over ACD is slight and shown without uncertainty. Forecasting performance therefore does not validate causal discovery or the claim that causality drives the improvement. These foundational theoretical and empirical issues prevent acceptance despite the useful problem formulation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored problem: causal discovery when interaction structure changes according to latent states.

The conditional summary graph is intuitive and potentially useful. Under the paper's source-local state assumption, it avoids explicitly representing K^N global regimes and gives interpretable state-dependent outgoing structures.
SDCI combines latent-state inference, amortized graph inference, and a GNN decoder in a flexible framework supporting observed, determined, and recurrent states as well as sample-specific graphs.

The evaluation is broad, spanning controlled physical simulations, semi-synthetic gene regulation, and NBA trajectories. Results include near-perfect recovery in the easiest synthetic setting, competitive variable-graph recovery, and the best reported GRN F1 score. The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and a code link.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability result does not follow under the stated assumptions. Theorem A.6 invokes finite-Gaussian-mixture identifiability after conditioning on the history, but no positive mixing-weight, full-support, or regime-overlap assumption is imposed. A never-visited state can have an arbitrary graph without changing the observed distribution, and K can be enlarged with such states. Deterministic state regions, central to the paper's determined-state setting, can likewise leave only one active component at each conditioning value. This directly undermines the claimed state-dependency-free and unknown-K guarantees.

The proof of edge-type identifiability in Corollary A.8 has another material gap. Permutation invariance of the aggregator does not imply equal partial derivatives with respect to different messages at unequal inputs; for example, a symmetric squared-sum function has message-dependent derivatives. Moreover, separation of edge functions within each model does not by itself identify products involving two unrestricted aggregators across observationally equivalent models. The claimed single global permutation of edge types is therefore unproven.

Appendix B.2's claimed O(NK) exact marginalization is generally invalid. With a nonlinear decoder applied after aggregating state-dependent messages, marginalizing the likelihood requires a joint sum over state configurations; the elementwise product in Equation 57 leaves the messages unintegrated and does not equal that marginal. Likewise, setting q(s|x) equal to the state-transition model is not generally exact posterior inference because subsequent observations also depend on the state.

The experiments only partially test the main contribution. Conditional-graph recovery is quantified only on the custom particle simulator and without a state-aware causal-discovery baseline. The principal baseline comparison and GRN experiment collapse conditional graphs to ordinary union graphs, while NBA provides only forecasting and qualitative, unverifiable edges; its improvement over the closest amortized baseline, ACD, is small.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are insufficiently documented: numbers of random runs, meanings of error bars, uncertainty or significance, permutation alignment for latent state and edge labels, graph thresholds, and several data-split details are missing. The GRN result appears to use one simulated network, and it is unclear whether NBA windows are split by game.

Some comparisons are structurally unfavorable to the baselines: SDCI learns an amortized inference mechanism from 10,000 simulated sequences, whereas Rhino and N-GC are retrained on each short sequence in the variable-graph setting. Rhino also uses a much smaller network. There are no adequate ablations or sensitivity analyses for K, the strong sparsity priors, state modeling, model capacity, or computational cost.

The advertised scope is broader than the actual model: states control only a source variable's outgoing effects, and the implemented state process is autonomous per node and conditioned on that node's own history. Together with first-order dynamics, no instantaneous effects or hidden confounding, Gaussian additive noise, and shared interaction types, this excludes motivating cases such as states driven by other agents' histories.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult setting: causal discovery when interactions change with latent, observation-dependent states. The conditional summary graph is an intuitive compact representation under the paper's source-conditioned factorization.

SDCI is a technically interesting extension of amortized causal discovery, combining state inference, discrete edge types, and graph-neural-network dynamics for observed, determined, and recurrent states.

The evaluation is unusually broad, spanning controlled particle systems, a semi-synthetic gene-regulatory model, and NBA trajectories. Results are promising in fixed-graph synthetic settings, and SDCI obtains the best reported GRN F1 score.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes substantial appendices covering proofs, architectures, training settings, datasets, and additional experiments. A code repository is provided.
The discussion appropriately acknowledges the exponential difficulty of recurrent-state inference and the absence of a consistency result for the learned variational estimator.
weaknesses: The principal identifiability theorem is not convincingly established. Theorem A.6 applies finite Gaussian-mixture identifiability pointwise while implicitly requiring every regime to have positive conditional probability. Assumptions (m1-m5) impose no positivity, reachability, or support condition; in the emphasized deterministic-state examples, weights are zero or one at each observation. Unused or locally absent regimes can therefore be altered without changing the observed distribution, invalidating identification of their graphs and of the number of regimes. The proof also does not adequately control permutations that may vary with the conditioning history.

The claimed identification of the unknown K is especially unsupported: the formal identifiability definitions already condition on K equaling the alternative model's K, while zero-weight or redundant regimes defeat the subsequent mixture argument. The two illustrative reconstruction-error curves do not constitute a reliable model-selection evaluation.

Theorem A.7 recovers each source node's state-indexed outgoing structures only up to a separate permutation for that node. Independent node-wise permutations can recombine outgoing edges into entirely different graphs, so this does not identify the globally aligned collection of conditional summary graphs claimed in the paper.

The edge-type result in Corollary A.8 contains a serious proof gap. Permutation invariance of an aggregator does not imply that its partial derivatives are equal at unequal message inputs or across targets, and equality of products of aggregator and message-function derivatives does not identify the individual edge types. Moreover, the required derivative conditions are not enforced by SDCI; the assertion that analyticity guarantees them is false, and the implemented MLPs need not satisfy them.

The claimed exact O(NK) inference for determined states is also questionable. With a nonlinear aggregator, marginalizing independent source states still requires a joint sum over their configurations; Equation 57 omits this coupling. In addition, p(s_t|x_t) is generally not the posterior p(s_t|x_1:T), because future observations contain information about s_t through the transition model. Thus setting q equal to the state prior is not exact except under an explicitly enforced deterministic mapping.

The empirical comparisons do not isolate causal or state-dependent structure recovery. Conditional graphs are reduced to union summary graphs for comparison mostly against stationary baselines, and the variable-graph experiments compare an amortized model trained over 10,000 trajectories with methods retrained from a single short trajectory. A parameter-matched switching or noncausal mixture-of-experts baseline is needed to distinguish the proposed causal structure from added gating and model capacity.

The evidence lacks repeated-run variability, statistical tests, and several essential evaluation details such as graph-threshold selection. The recurrent variable-graph setting remains relatively weak. On the sparse GRN, SDCI's best F1 is only 0.347 and its AUROC is essentially tied with Rhino; AUPRC and results across multiple simulated networks are needed.

The NBA experiment has no causal ground truth, uses hand-designed or position-determined states, and shows only a small forecasting advantage over ACD without uncertainty estimates. Qualitatively plausible learned edges and improved prediction do not demonstrate causal discovery or establish that causality drives the forecasting gain.

The advertised scope is broader than the supported setting: the analysis assumes first-order dynamics, no instantaneous effects or hidden confounding, Gaussian additive noise, unique state-specific outgoing structures, and source-local pairwise mechanisms. Several experimental systems are not shown to satisfy these assumptions.
